## Recap

::: {.justify}

In the last chapter, we

- Compared observed mortality rates with [**standard mortality rates**]{.alert} using standardised mortality ratios.
- Used the [**chi-squared test**]{.alert} to assess whether the standard rates could explain the observed deaths across age groups.
- Considered the [**cumulative deviations test**]{.secondary} and the [**sign test**]{.secondary} for detecting bias, and discussed the risks of multiple testing.

:::

# <span style="font-size: 42px; color: #131516; display: block; margin-bottom: -50px">[**Chapter 16**]{.secondary}: Graduation</span>

## Graduation

:::: {.justify .small-text}

We expect the true underlying mortality rate in a population to vary smoothly with age.

::: {.fragment}

An estimated mortality rate

$$
\hat m_x=\frac{D_x}{E_x^C}
$$

is an observation of a random variable, with distribution centred on the true underlying mortality rate, but subject to variation quantified by its asymptotic variance $m_x/E_x^C$. This variance may be large when the exposure $E_x^C$ is small.

:::

::: {.fragment}

[**Graduation**]{.alert} is the term actuaries and demographers use for the statistical [**smoothing**]{.secondary} of estimated mortality rates, to obtain a more realistic picture of how mortality changes with age.

:::

::::

## Example

::: {.justify .small-text}

This is an expanded version of the example used in [**Chapter 15**]{.secondary}, where now we observe age groups $x=60,\cdots,89$.

```{r}
#| label: graduation-setup
#| include: false

have_data <- file.exists("data/ELT16.csv")

if (have_data) {
  set.seed(270966)
  elt <- read.csv("data/ELT16.csv")
  names(elt) <- c("x", "e", "d", "y", "g")
  elt <- elt[match(60:89, elt$x), ]
  stopifnot(!anyNA(elt$x))

  elt$e <- round(elt$e / 1000, 1)
  elt$d <- rbinom(30, elt$d, 1 / 1000)
  elt$d[1:10] <- c(8, 10, 5, 8, 13, 16, 18, 12, 14, 11)
  elt$m <- c(
    0.00794, 0.00863, 0.00949, 0.01019, 0.01100,
    0.01199, 0.01330, 0.01479, 0.01586, 0.01781,
    0.02030, 0.02242, 0.02510, 0.02698, 0.03009,
    0.03306, 0.03703, 0.04049, 0.04599, 0.05093,
    0.05754, 0.06516, 0.07427, 0.08320, 0.09284,
    0.10457, 0.11749, 0.13113, 0.14720, 0.16530
  )
}

plot_graduation <- function(data, graduated = NULL, standard = NULL) {
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0),
                 mar = c(3.2, 3.6, 0.8, 0.6))
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  raw <- data$d / data$e

  draw <- function(transform, ylab) {
    y <- transform(raw)
    z <- if (!is.null(graduated)) transform(graduated) else NULL
    s <- if (!is.null(standard)) transform(standard) else NULL

    plot(data$x, y, xlab = "Age (x)", ylab = ylab,
         ylim = range(c(y, z, s), finite = TRUE),
         bty = "l", las = 1)

    if (!is.null(s)) points(data$x, s, pch = 3)
    if (!is.null(z)) points(data$x, z, pch = 2)
  }

  draw(identity, expression(hat(m)[x]))
  draw(log, expression(log(hat(m)[x])))
}
```

::: {style="margin-top: 15pt;"}
:::

Plots of the raw estimated mortality rates on the original and log scales.

::: {style="margin-top: 25pt;"} 
:::

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.75, fig.align = "center"}
if (have_data) {
  plot_graduation(elt)
} else {
  cat("Place ELT16.csv alongside this deck to reproduce the plots and fits.")
}
```

:::

## Graduation methods

:::: {.justify .small-text}

There are three main approaches to graduation, all of which involve fitting a statistical model.

::: {.fragment}

- Graduation against a set of [**standard mortality rates**]{.alert}.

  This is used where we have good reason to expect our study population to share features with the mortality experience of the standard population.

:::

::: {.fragment}

- Graduation using a [**parametric model**]{.alert}.

  This is usually used where we have large amounts of data.

:::

::: {.fragment}

- Graduation using a [**semiparametric (smooth) regression model**]{.alert}.

  This is usually used where we have small amounts of data and no suitable standard mortality rates.

:::

::::

## Graduation against a set of standard rates

:::: {.justify .small-text}

The simplest approach is to fit a regression-type model, such as

$$
D_x\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(E_x^C m_x),
\qquad
\log m_x=\beta_0+\beta_1\log m_x^S.
$$

::: {.fragment}

This is a [**generalised linear model**]{.alert} (GLM), which is easy to fit in software such as `R`. The graduated mortality rates are the maximum likelihood estimates, given by

$$
\log\tilde m_x=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\log m_x^S.
$$

:::

::: {.fragment}

If the standard rates are smooth, as they typically will have been previously graduated, then the estimated rates will be smooth too.

Students taking [**MATH3091**]{.secondary} will learn more about generalised linear models.

:::

::::

## Return to the example

::: {.justify .small-text}

Graduation against standard rates. The plot shows the [**raw rates**]{.alert} [**(circles)**]{.secondary}, [**standard rates**]{.alert} [**(crosses)**]{.secondary} and [**graduated rates**]{.alert} [**(triangles)**]{.secondary} on the original and log scales.

::: {style="margin-top: 25pt;"} 
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3, fig.align = "center"}
if (have_data) {
  # See how the model is fitted
  fit_standard <- glm(d ~ log(m) + offset(log(e)), data = elt, family = poisson())
  plot_graduation(elt, graduated = fitted(fit_standard) / elt$e, standard = elt$m)
}
```

:::

## Graduation using a parametric model

:::: {.justify .small-text}

This approach assumes that there is a parametric formula describing the relationship between the central mortality rate and age.

The simplest model is the [**log-linear Gompertz model**]{.alert}.

$$
D_x\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(E_x^C m_x),
\qquad
\log m_x=\beta_0+\beta_1 x.
$$

::: {.fragment}

This is a [**GLM**.]{.secondary} The graduated mortality rates are the maximum likelihood estimates, given by

$$
\log\tilde m_x=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x.
$$

The estimated rates vary smoothly with age.

:::

::: {.fragment}

More complex Gompertz models replace $\beta_0+\beta_1x$ with a polynomial 
$$
\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\cdots+\beta_px^p.
$$ 
These are also [**GLMs**.]{.secondary}

:::

::::

## Return to the example

::: {.justify .small-text}

Graduation using the [**log-linear Gompertz model**.]{.alert} The plot shows the [**raw rates**]{.alert} [**(circles)**]{.secondary} and [**graduated rates**]{.alert} [**(triangles)**]{.secondary} on the original and log scales.

::: {style="margin-top: 25pt;"} 
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3, fig.align = "center"}
if (have_data) {
  # See how the model is fitted
  fit_gompertz <- glm(d ~ x + offset(log(e)), data = elt, family = poisson())
  plot_graduation(elt, graduated = fitted(fit_gompertz) / elt$e)
}
```

:::

## Models for human mortality

:::: {.justify .small-text}

A general Gompertz model

$$
\log m_x=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx^j
$$

is often found to fit mortality at higher ages well, for quite small values of $p$, such as $p=1$ (linear model with two parameters) or $p=2$ (quadratic model with three parameters).

::: {.fragment}

If necessary, the Gompertz model can be extended to the [**Gompertz-Makeham family**]{.alert}, which has

$$
m_x=\alpha_0+\sum_{j=1}^q\alpha_jx^j+
\exp\!\left(\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx^j\right).
$$

This model is [**no** longer a GLM]{.secondary} and is less straightforward to fit.

:::

::::

## Graduation using a semiparametric model

:::: {.justify .small-text}

This approach estimates the underlying mortality rates by balancing fit to the data and smoothness of the underlying function.

::: {.fragment}

The resulting model is called a [**generalised additive model**]{.alert} [**(GAM)**]{.secondary} and can be written as

$$
D_x\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(E_x^C m_x),
\qquad
\log m_x=s(x),
$$

where $s(x)$ denotes a smooth function of $x$.

:::

::: {.fragment}

A [**GAM**]{.secondary} is fitted by minimising an objective function that balances fit to the data (for example, the negative log-likelihood) and smoothness (for example, the integrated squared second derivative).

:::

::::

## Return to the example

::: {.justify .small-text}

Graduation using the [**semiparametric model**.]{.alert} The plot shows the [**raw rates**]{.alert} [**(circles)**]{.secondary} and [**graduated rates**]{.alert} [**(triangles)**]{.secondary} on the original and log scales.

::: {style="margin-top: 25pt;"} 
:::

```{r, echo = TRUE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3, fig.align = "center"}
if (have_data & requireNamespace("gam", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # See how the model is fitted
  fit_smooth <- gam::gam(d ~ gam::s(x) + offset(log(e)), data = elt, family = poisson())
  plot_graduation(elt, graduated = fitted(fit_smooth) / elt$e)
} else if (have_data) { cat("Install the `gam` package to reproduce the semiparametric fit.") }
```

:::

## Testing the fit of a graduation

:::: {.justify .small-text}

A set of graduated mortality rates should be compared with the original rates to check the fit of the graduation.

The chi-squared test described in [**Chapter 15**]{.secondary} can be used for this, with test statistic

$$
X^2=\sum_x\frac{(D_x-E_x^C\tilde m_x)^2}{E_x^C\tilde m_x},
\tag{1}
$$

where $\tilde m_x$ are the graduated rates.

::: {.fragment}

[A minor modification is required.]{.alert} The components of the sum in [**Equation $(1)$**]{.secondary} are no longer independent because the $D_x$ have been used to obtain the graduated rates $\tilde m_x$.

:::

::: {.fragment}

Deduct one degree of freedom (from $v$) for each estimated parameter. If we have estimated $p$ parameters across $v$ age groups, the reference distribution is approximately $\chi^2_{v-p}$. 

The other tests in [**Chapter 15**]{.secondary} do not have a simple adjustment for testing the fit of a graduation, and therefore should be avoided.

:::

::::

## Return to the example

:::: {.justify .small-text}

For the graduations illustrated in Sections [**Section 16.3.1**]{.secondary}, [**Section 16.4.1**]{.secondary}, and  [**Section 16.5.2**]{.secondary}, respectively, we have

- $X^2 = 31.74:$ graduation against standard rates
- $X^2 = 28.20:$ graduation using Gompertz log-linear model
- $X^2 = 25.84:$ graduation using semiparametric (smooth) model

:::{.fragment}

The number of age groups is $v = 30$ and the number of parameters is $p = 2$ for the first two models and $p = 3.0$ (an estimated function of the overall smoothness) for the semiparametric model.

:::

:::{.fragment}

So we compare our $X^2$ values with the $95\%$ point of $\chi^2_{28}$ $(41.34)$ and the $95\%$ point of $\chi^2_{27}$ $(40.11)$.

:::

:::{.fragment}

We see that there is no evidence to lead us to reject the fit of the graduated rates to the observed rates, so all three of the graduations seem satisfactory.

:::
